content: Asymptomatic bacteriuria, which is defined as the presence of bacteria in the urine without any signs or symptoms of a urinary tract infection (UTI), is observed in 17% to 51% of kidney transplant recipients. It is hypothesized that this condition may increase the risk of developing a symptomatic UTI. However, there is no consensus regarding the use of antibiotics to treat asymptomatic bacteriuria in kidney transplant patients. The objective of this review was to evaluate the potential benefits and harms of using antimicrobial agents to treat asymptomatic bacteriuria in kidney transplant recipients. Specifically, the review aimed to determine whether such treatment could prevent symptomatic UTIs, reduce all-cause mortality, and mitigate indirect complications of UTIs, such as acute rejection, graft loss, or deterioration of graft function. The search for relevant studies was conducted in the Cochrane Kidney and Transplant Register of Studies up to September 1, 2017. This register includes studies identified through searches of CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, conference proceedings, the International Clinical Trials Register (ICTRP) Search Portal, and ClinicalTrials.gov. The review included all randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-RCTs, regardless of language, that assessed the treatment of asymptomatic bacteriuria in kidney transplant recipients at any time after transplantation. Two independent authors evaluated the eligibility of studies, assessed their quality, and extracted data. The primary outcomes of interest were the incidence of symptomatic UTI and the development of antimicrobial resistance. Secondary outcomes included all-cause mortality, graft loss, graft rejection, graft function, hospitalization due to UTI, adverse reactions to antimicrobial agents, and the persistence or recurrence of asymptomatic bacteriuria. Dichotomous outcomes were expressed as absolute risk differences (RD) or risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI), while continuous data were reported as mean differences (MD) with 95% CI. Data were pooled using a random-effects model. The review included two studies with a total of 212 participants that compared antibiotic treatment to no treatment. Additionally, three ongoing studies were identified. In the groups that did not receive treatment for asymptomatic bacteriuria, the incidence of symptomatic UTI ranged from 19% to 31%. The effect of antibiotic treatment on preventing symptomatic UTI was uncertain (2 studies, 200 participants: RR 0.86, 95% CI 0.51 to 1.45). Similarly, the risk of selecting multidrug-resistant organisms with antibiotic treatment was unclear (1 study, 112 participants: RR 1.21, 95% CI 0.60 to 2.41). Persistence of asymptomatic bacteriuria was high regardless of whether antibiotics were used. The effects of antibiotics on other important outcomes, such as all-cause mortality (1 study, 112 participants: RR 2.23, 95% CI 0.21 to 23.86), graft loss (1 study, 112 participants: RR 1.11, 95% CI 0.07 to 17.36), acute rejection (1 study, 112 participants: RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.44 to 1.97), hospitalization for UTI (1 study, 112 participants: RR 0.74, 95% CI 0.13 to 4.27), graft function (2 studies, 200 participants, MD in serum creatinine concentration -0.06 mg/dL, 95% CI -0.19 to 0.08), and adverse reactions (1 study, 112 participants: no severe adverse events attributable to antibiotic treatment) were also uncertain. The quality of evidence for all outcomes was rated as low. In conclusion, there is currently insufficient evidence to recommend the routine use of antibiotics to treat asymptomatic bacteriuria in kidney transplant recipients. The available data are limited, and further research is needed to clarify the potential benefits and risks of this approach. The results of three ongoing randomized studies are awaited and may help address the existing uncertainties.
